proposition: The fort counts of the Rigveda are formulaic quantities drawn from a small stock of culturally salient numbers, not an enumeration of a remembered number of strongholds.
rests_on_claims: PUR4J-002; PUR4J-003; PUR4J-006; PUR4J-007; PUR4J-008; PUR4J-009
evidence_for: Four diagnostic predictions were set before the evidence was read, and three are met decisively. (1) An enumeration should be stable per opponent. It is not: Sambara's forts are counted at 90, 99, 100, 'the hundredth' and 'hundreds' across six passages (PUR4J-007) - every value the constitution enumerates, on one opponent. (2) An enumeration should not migrate to a different class of object. It does: the identical nava-plus-navati- expression counts ninety-nine RIVERS at RV 10.104.8 (PUR4J-006). (3) An enumeration should not be systematically completed by a round number. It is: two of the six ninety-nine passages append 'the hundredth' (PUR4J-008), so the 99 is functioning as one-short-of-a-hundred. (4) An enumeration should occasionally produce an irregular figure. None does: every count is 7, 90, 99, 100 or 'hundreds' (PUR4J-009), across 21 passages, ten books and every Arnold stratum.
evidence_against: One prediction is NOT met, and it is recorded here rather than in a footnote. The numbers are not freely interchangeable ornament: they are distributed by narrative cycle (PUR4J-010). Seven forts go with Purukutsa and the Puru in all four of their passages, in wording that is near-verbatim at RV 1.174.2b and 6.20.10c; ninety-nine and one hundred go with Divodasa, Atithigva and Sambara. A purely ornamental number should not sort by story. What the evidence supports is a formula system with slots filled by cycle, which is a weaker and more specific claim than 'the numbers are meaningless'.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does NOT establish that no fortification underlies any passage, and it must not be read that way. A formulaic count can be attached to a real siege; the number being conventional says nothing about whether anything was besieged. It also does not establish that the counts are late, invented, or purely literary. Constitution section 4J puts 'poetic formula' and 'textual stronghold' in a five-way typology precisely because a passage can be assessed on both axes, and the typology is assigned per passage in 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-typology.csv - never inherited from this row.
falsifier: A passage stating an irregular count of forts (say 23, or 41) would break PUR4J-009 and weaken the whole reading. A second corpus-external attestation of a specific fort count tied to a specific place would move the question out of the text. Demonstrating that nava-navati- at RV 10.104.8 is a scribal or editorial intrusion would remove the migration evidence, though not the Sambara instability. Conversely, finding that the ninety-nine passages share a single poet lineage would strengthen the formula reading by localising it.

notes: PROVISIONAL, not VERIFIED: the underlying counts are verified measurements, but the step from them to 'formulaic' is a reading. Held at PROVISIONAL rather than promoted, because the reading is CONVENIENT - it is the deflationary answer, it flatters a sceptical posture, and it costs nothing to assert. The preferred-counter-narrative test in 04-AUDITS/rigveda-pur-4j-method.md section 8 was run specifically against this row.

proposition: The prominence of ninety-nine in modern citation of the Rigvedic forts is a fact about reception, not a property of the corpus.
evidence_for: Ninety-nine is the second most frequent fort count in the corpus (6 passages against 8 for one hundred, PUR4J-003), it is not the largest, and it is not expressed by a numeral of its own (PUR4J-004). Nothing in the distribution singles it out. It is nevertheless the figure that titles the inherited RV-01 specification, the the-forts page headline, and Version 12 lines 1114, 1164, 1169, 1175 and 1272.
evidence_against: Ninety-nine is a genuinely distinctive expression in a way that one hundred is not: 100 is the ordinary Vedic 'very many' and occurs 14 times in these passages in all functions, while nava-navati- is marked and memorable. Griffith's rendering 'nine-and-ninety castles' is a striking English phrase and is the wording most likely to have carried the number into anglophone circulation. So the salience is not arbitrary - it is a property of the expression, not of the count.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does NOT establish where MelaKeela's ninety-nine came from. No source is recorded for the the-forts headline anywhere in this repository, and the curatorial audit rates it Medium risk, 'thin or undetected bibliography', 'Revise before release'. The transmission path proposed here - through Griffith's English - is untested and no retrieval was attempted against it.
falsifier: A document showing that MelaKeela's ninety-nine was derived from a corpus operation rather than from the text's numerals would overturn 06-BRIEFS/rv01-reconciliation.md section 2.6 and this row with it. A pre-Griffith English source giving the number would move the proposed transmission path.
notes: The prestige-bias test cuts both ways here and both were run. Demoting 99 because it arrives in a page headline rather than a commit hash would be the error the reconciliation brief warned against; 99 is now a VERIFIED count of six passages, with locators, and outranks the register's 106 on the question of how many forts a passage names. What is demoted is only its claim to be THE number, and that demotion is a measurement.

proposition: The Rigvedic pur- corpus does not describe a single kind of object, and no single English word or archaeological referent can stand for it.
rests_on_claims: PUR4J-013; PUR4J-020; PUR4J-021; PUR4J-022; PUR4J-025; PUR4J-027
evidence_for: Five independent measurements converge. (1) Case: 67.5 percent of simplex tokens are accusative and 3.6 percent locative — the pur is overwhelmingly a thing broken, almost never a place anyone is in. (2) Typology: 46 of 103 passages are figurative and 3 more are both, so very nearly half the corpus is not describing a fort at all — 28 of them divine epithets, lexical (puramdara-) or analytic (puram bhindur). (3) Material: 8 of the 10 passages stating a material are figurative or unclassifiable, and in two of them the pur IS a god or a river. (4) Descriptors: one pur is carisnu- 'moving' (RV 8.1.28) and one is ama- 'raw, unbaked' (RV 2.35.6). (5) Lexicography: Grassmann defines the word as an earthwork — 'Wall aus Steinen und Lehm, Verschanzung, Palisade' — and no translator in the corpus renders it 'city' more than once in 103 passages.
evidence_against: The corpus is not uniformly figurative either, and this is the half that a deflationary reading drops. 49 of 103 passages present a fort as an object in the narrative; all six ninety-nine passages and all four seven-fort passages are among them; the forts have named holders (Sambara, Pipru, Vangrda, Varcin), stated materials in two enemy cases (stone at RV 4.30.20, metal at RV 2.20.8), a gate (RV 6.18.5), and possibly a proper name (RV 1.149.3, disputed). Whatever else the corpus is doing, it is also describing things that were held and broken.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does NOT establish what a pur was, whether any corresponded to a built structure, or where any stood. It bears on the FORM of the answer — that the answer will be plural — not on its content. Specifically it does not license the inverse error of concluding that no Rigvedic pur was a real fortification: 49 passages present one as an object, and this unit has no evidence bearing on whether any of them stood anywhere.
falsifier: A demonstration that the figurative passages are chronologically or dialectally separable from the narrative ones would replace this with a two-stage account rather than a plural one. A retrieved archaeological or geographic argument tied to a specific passage would move the three unassigned types out of NOT ASSIGNED for that passage and change what the corpus can be asked. Settling the ayas- crux (PUR4J-023) would sharpen point 3 considerably.
